films.title: Life Is Cheap... But Toilet Paper Is Expensive
intro: Experience one of Wayne Wang’s (The Joy Luck Club, Smoke, Blue in the Face) early masterpieces with a brand new electronic score by producer & DJ Yu Su.

Exploding a seemingly simple premise – a nameless “cowboy” courier (Spencer Nakasako) arrives in pre-Handover Hong Kong to deliver a mysterious briefcase to a mercurial Mob boss whilst becoming entangled with his femme fatale mistress (Cora Miao) – independent filmmaking legend Wayne Wang’s Life Is Cheap… But Toilet Paper Is Expensive barrels through inspired genre deconstruction, guerrilla docu-fiction and fierce political jeremiad, all with a keen sense of humor and one of the richest visual palettes of the 1990s.
description: Tracking the Man-with-no-name’s increasingly byzantine mission across every level of the city’s social strata, we’re introduced to fortune families, cabdrivers, hustlers, butchers and more, each punctuating the high-octane Neo-noir narrative with instantly memorable monologues that capture a now-distant era in Hong Kong history.

Multifaceted but never incoherent Life Is Cheap… But Toilet Paper Is Expensive is among Wang’s most unique and bracing contributions to the independent film cannon. Much-loved on the 90s international film festival circuit but unjustly overlooked in North America, this is a maverick tour de force ripe for rediscovery.

Born in Kaifeng and currently based in London, Yu Su is a multifaceted artist known for her work as a musician, DJ, and creative chef. Her music uniquely blends dubby textures with left-field dance elements. She has released tracks on renowned labels, including the UK's Technicolor, the Netherlands' Music from Memory, and China's Bie Records, earning critical acclaim and a nomination for the prestigious Polaris Prize in Canada. Yu has collaborated with notable artists such as John Carroll Kirby and Duval Timothy, and she is recognised for her remixes of tracks for well-known bands like Parquet Courts and King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard. Her intuitive DJ sets have garnered international attention, leading to performances at prominent clubs and festivals, including Dekmantel, Glastonbury, Boiler Room, iii Points, Nuits Sonores, Rainbow Disco Club, Panorama Bar, and Phonox.

Yu transforms dancefloors into ethereal spaces where rhythms stretch and dissolve, fluidly moving between experimental pulses and powerful currents to create an unforced, transformative experience. Her second album Foundry comes out May 1st, 2026 on Short Span Records featuring Seefeel, Dip in the pool and Memotone.

films.title: The Blind Couple from Mali
intro: For decades, Amadou & Mariam turned their blindness and life in Mali into a remarkable musical journey. Their fame spread far beyond Africa, while their love endured for nearly half a century. The Blind Couple from Mali looks back at their extraordinary partnership, from Bamako to Amadou’s death in 2025, with rare intimate footage.
description: Amadou Bagayoko passed away on 4 April 2025. This marked the end of a relationship with Mariam Doumbia that had lasted almost fifty years. The blind Malian couple also formed a musical duo. They had been releasing music as Amadou & Mariam since the late 1980s, but it took ten years before they made their breakthrough in Europe and became one of the best-selling African music acts. In 2024, they performed Gainsbourg’s Je suis venu te dire que je m’en vais at the closing ceremony of the Olympic Games in Paris. As it turned out, this was their final public performance. In The Blind Couple from Mali, director Ryan Marley tells their story, from their first meeting at the Institut des Jeunes Aveugles in Bamako right up to Amadou’s passing. What is also remarkable is that he was present during the recording of their final album in 2023. The Blind Couple from Mali paints a captivating portrait of these two warm-hearted people whose vibrant lives lay at the crossroads of music and love.

films.title: Krakatoa
intro: Born from the cataclysmic 1883 eruption of Krakatoa, this immersive journey follows Kesuma, a castaway struggling to survive on a remote island. As isolation and nature reshape his world, reality gives way to something dreamlike and elemental. Rich in sound and atmosphere, the film becomes a sensory meditation on humanity’s fragile place within the natural world.
description: In 1883, the volcano Krakatoa erupted on the East Asian island of the same name in the Sunda Strait. The bang that accompanied it is the loudest ever recorded, audible from 4700 km away. Five months later, a large part of the island had been swallowed by the waves. That historic event is the starting point of Krakatoa, the new film by Spanish experimental director and visual artist Carlos Casas. The protagonist is the reserved Kesuma, who is flung into the ocean when his raft is caught up in the eruption and washes up on a lonely island where he tries to survive. His struggle against nature nonetheless transforms into a psychedelic trip through which Casas explores humanity's fragile bond with our planet. Albeit in a way that you have to hear, feel and see, more than understand. Featuring superb sound design by Nicolas Becker, who won an Oscar for his work on Sound of Metal.

intro: After the success of Saint Frances and Ghostlight, co-directors Kelly O’Sullivan and Alex Thompson once again display their mastery in depicting loss, grief and a (renewed) search for identity in their third co-production Mouse. This coming-of-age drama is a modest and wholesome gem, following Minnie who needs to find her way in life without her best friend.
description: They are as different as night and day, the 17-year-old teenage girls Callie and Minnie. The former is spending her final days at secondary school in Arkansas, dreaming of a Broadway career, whilst being admired and envied by her many friends. The latter is a shy maths whizz who feels safe in the shadow of her charismatic best friend. The two are inseparable, until a tragic car accident brings their friendship to an abrupt end. Minnie feels utterly lost now that she must face the growing pains of adolescence alone. The only ally she seems to find in her boundless grief is Callie’s mother, Helen. From their shared sorrow emerges a tender yet complex dynamic, which complicates Minnie’s search for her own identity. Mouse manages to strike a balance between humour and intense grief, though you’ll certainly need plenty of tissues whilst watching this deeply human drama.

films.title: I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming
intro: The relationship of a young queer Ukrainian couple is put to the test when one partner’s gender transition collides with Russia’s full-scale invasion. Rooted in reality, this timely and tender film centers on living and loving on the edge of the abyss, and the struggle to safeguard one’s identity amid extreme violence.
description: While Olya (Tania Myronyshena) and Oleh (Markus Bright) are dealing with the internal tensions surrounding Oleh's recent gender transition, they must also contend with unprecedented cruelty from outside when Russia invades Ukraine at the same time. The fiercely topical I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming was largely filmed in and around Kyiv and draws on the experiences of the circle of friends of Ukrainian screenwriter Anna Melikova and German filmmaker Isabelle Stever. Rooted in reality, they explore how the war takes over everyday life and increasingly narrows the boundaries of masculinity and femininity. The violence of war is ever-present, yet never shown directly. The focus is on a couple who go to the utmost lengths to save their freedom and identity from an all-consuming wartime reality. Every shot bears witness to a deep belief in the political power of cinema.

films.title: Nostalgia for the Future
intro: Who was Chris Marker, really? The enigmatic filmmaker behind La Jetée spent a lifetime hiding behind pseudonyms, images and cats. In Nostalgia for the Future, Brecht Debackere dives into his vast archive, with Charlotte Rampling as his guide. An idiosyncratic, essayistic journey through Marker’s legacy and what images preserve of us after we are gone.
description: Chris Marker disliked portraits. The French filmmaker behind La Jetée and Sans Soleil was rarely photographed, worked under pseudonyms and was quite happy to be represented by the image of a cat. After his death, however, he left behind a staggering archive. In Nostalgia for the Future, an archivist wanders through this material legacy in search of the man who spent his entire life carefully keeping himself out of sight. For eight years, Belgian artist and filmmaker Brecht Debackere immersed himself in Marker’s world. Guided by the enigmatic voice of Charlotte Rampling, he allows photographs, writings and film fragments to speak once again. The result is not a conventional artist portrait, but an idiosyncratic cinematic puzzle in which past and present constantly intertwine. For how much of a person truly remains in their images? And can those images, as Marker himself so often did, look towards the future?

films.title: Revolutionaries Never Die (الثوار لا يموتون أبدًا)
intro: A chance invitation from Lebanese film pioneer Jocelyne Saab sets Mohanad Yaqubi on an unexpected path years later. After devastating parallels link Saab’s story to his own family history in Gaza, he creates a cinematic letter exploring her work from 1973 to 1983 while reflecting on memory, loss, resistance and the Palestinian experience today.
description: Coincidences that are more than coincidences: Belgian-Palestinian filmmaker Mohanad Yaqubi has experienced it himself. At the end of 2018, he received an invitation from Jocelyne Saab to collaborate. She was a filmmaker regarded as one of the founders of modern Lebanese cinema. Was, indeed, because a few months after that invitation, Saab died. In one of her most famous documentaries, Beirut My City, she stands in front of her 150-year-old family home, which was destroyed in an Israeli attack. Yaqubi’s childhood home in Gaza was bombed by the same army in 2024. This happened just days before he was due to introduce Saab’s film at Cinematek. Because coincidences do not exist, Yaqubi decided to write a cinematic letter to Saab, Revolutionaries Never Die, focusing on her work between 1973 and 1983. The documentary is a tribute to Saab and an exploration of her films, but it also offers a portrait of the Palestinian struggle.

films.title: Historias extraordinarias (Extraordinary Stories)

intro: Gauchos, the Latin American version of the cowboy, know better than anyone that the joy of travelling lies in getting lost. The same is true of X, Z and H, the protagonists of Mariano Llinás’s monumental tour de force, each of whom loses their way on whimsical, adventurous wanderings across the Argentine pampas.
description: X witnesses a murder and becomes entangled in a web of conspiracies. Z takes a job in a sleepy provincial town and delves into his predecessor’s secret past. H sails down the Salado River in search of the remains of a forgotten engineering project. These could well be the makings of cheap novels – and Gabriel Chwojnik’s playful, pulpy soundtrack reveals just how deliberately the film flirts with the tradition of adventure novels and gritty detective fiction. Yet Mariano Llinás uses these pulp ingredients for something bolder: a cheerful assault on the conventions of cinema. Like a mischievous rebel, he knocks them down and uses the rubble to build a majestic labyrinth of mysteries. Thus, Historias extraordinarias becomes not only an ode to Argentina, but also to a land without borders: that of the imagination. The viewer has no choice but to surrender to the pulsating power of the story.

intro: Starting from a classic premise – an inexplicable disappearance – Laura Citarella constructs an ever-expanding universe full of enigmas. description: When the passionate botanist Laura vanishes without a trace, her boyfriend and colleague set out on a search through the Argentine pampas. But every clue leads to a new mystery. Chapter by chapter, filmmaker Laura Citarella unfolds her story as a cinematic narrative puzzle in which each new perspective undermines the previous one. What begins as a detective story about a missing woman branches out into secret love letters, a rare flower and a monster in a lake. Citarella, a key figure in the idiosyncratic collective El Pampero Cine, constructs a universe in which Jorge Luis Borges wanders into an Argentine version of Twin Peaks. Following screenings at Venice and Film Fest Gent (FFG22), Trenque Lauquen went on to become one of the most acclaimed films of that year: Cahiers du Cinéma even crowned Citarella’s four-hour epic the best film of 2023.

films.title: Pin de Fartie
sections: Focus on: El Pampero Cine: Infinite Stories
intro: A blind man and a girl, two stage actors, a mother and her son. Three pairs of characters search for meaning in the finitude of things. Endgame, Samuel Beckett's masterpiece for the theatre, takes on multiple forms in Pin de Fartie. Inspired director Alejo Moguillansky plays with expectations in what he describes as a film about infinite tenderness and peaceful horror.
description: Absurdist, minimalist, tragicomic. Samuel Beckett’s brilliant play Endgame is approaching its seventieth anniversary, yet continues to inspire audiences worldwide. This is demonstrated by Pin de Fartie, a play on words based on the French title of the play, Fin de partie, referring to the end of a game of chess. The internationally acclaimed Argentine filmmaker Alejo Moguillansky weaves together three surprising variations on the original, accompanied by a musician and a narrator, his partner Luciana Acuña. There are also roles for their daughter Cleo and Moguillansky himself, as the son of a blind pianist. He does not call it an adaptation, but “A film about a homeland once called Cinema”. The result is playful, yet defies convention; it is free, yet by no means without commitment. At its heart are still characters who explore the (im)possibility of relating to one another. Can their existential resistance avert the inevitable end?

imdb.title: Pin de Fartie
imdb.plot: A blind man and his daughter navigate their bond. Two actors find connection while rehearsing Endgame. A man reading Beckett to his blind mother realizes the play mirrors their relationship.

films.title: Le Faux Soir
intro: Faking a newspaper to outwit the Nazis: it sounds like the premise of an outrageous heist, but in occupied Brussels, it really happened. A group of resistance fighters produces a spoof edition of Le Soir, virtually indistinguishable from the real thing, that mercilessly mocks the occupiers. Michaël R. Roskam (Bullhead, 2011) brings this nearly forgotten act of resistance back to life as a gripping historical thriller brimming with audacity, dark humour and Brussels wit. A remarkable chapter of Belgian history about propaganda, the power of the media and the battle for truth that, more than eighty years later, has lost none of its urgency.
description: No bullets, but printer's ink: Le Faux Soir turns humour and imagination into weapons in the struggle for truth.

films.title: Chronovisor
intro: Chronovisor, the daring indie debut by Kevin Walker and Jack Auen, is an armchair mystery about a reclusive scholar and a device that can reveal the past. Blending science fiction, history and investigation, the film draws on the legend of the chronovisor - a machine said to make the past visible - and features music by Gustav Holst.
description: Following its premiere at the International Film Festival Rotterdam, Chronovisor was widely praised by critics. In short: the most intriguing, most daring American indie debut in years. This debut film by Kevin Walker and Jack Auen is an armchair mystery, a detective story in which the emphasis lies not on forensic investigation or action, but on solving an intellectual puzzle. Much like Agatha Christie’s work, though the plot of Chronovisor is far more flamboyant: the story of a reclusive professor (the debut role of French academic Anne-Laure Sellier!) and of a mysterious technology capable of revealing the past! Science fiction? Certainly, but based on the account of a monk who, in the 1970s, claimed to have witnessed the crucifixion of Christ through his alleged invention, the chronovisor. A thought-provoking film with nods to film history, set to the music of Gustav Holst.

films.title: Biografía de Jorge Luis Borges (Life of Jorge Luis Borges)
sections: Focus on: El Pampero Cine: Infinite Stories
intro: A mad genius or a genius madman? Director Mariano Llinás delves into the life of his beloved master, Argentine writer Jorge Luis Borges, one of the greatest literary icons of the 20th century. But how do you capture a writer who could conjure entire worlds with a single sentence? Part detective film, part road movie, over five hours long and unmistakably Llinás.
description: When filmmaker Mariano Llinás is enticed by the owners of Jorge Luis Borges’ private archive to make a documentary about the literary giant, he approaches this monumental undertaking in true Pampero fashion: as a wild expedition through Borges’ universe. Together with Ernesto Montequin, the stoic Borges-expert writing a book about the collection, he delves into the writer’s life and work. Drawing on diary fragments, unpublished poems, cryptic scribbles and notes, he attempts to get a grasp on his fellow countryman: that elusive writer who inspired the 20th century with his riddles, forking paths and endless labyrinths. As Llinás travels the world in search of traces and ghosts, a portrait emerges of the man, history and literature. Always playful and erudite, but with a healthy dose of self-deprecation, Llinás avoids the pitfalls of hagiography and happily loses himself in the shadowy paradoxes of a turbulent 20th century.
The film will be screened in 3 parts, with 2 intermissions during the screening.

films.title: Chicas tristes (Sad Girlz)
intro: Summer beckons promisingly by the pool, where La Maestra and Paula are training intensively to be selected for a championship. Even when they’re not doing laps, the best friends are found spending their time together by going plane-spotting, waiting for a solar eclipse or colourfully chalking the sidewalks of Mexico City. Their friendship however transforms when Paula becomes the victim of sexual violence at a party. In her impressive debut film, Mexican filmmaker Fernanda Tovar focuses on La Maestra’s gentle but clumsy attempts to help Paula deal with her trauma. Tovar emphasises the colour in her characters’ lives and, despite the darkness, has them bathing in a sea of light.
description: Tovar portrays with tact and determination how life continues unabated regardless of the injustice and suffering that befall us.

films.title: Queen at Sea
intro: The destructive nature of dementia has been a source of inspiration for many a filmmaker, but perhaps never quite as unvarnished, carnal and discomforting as in Lance Hammer’s Queen At Sea. Eighteen years after his lauded debut Ballast, the independent director returns with a gut-wrenching drama that questions our understanding of intimacy and sexuality, agency and care. In it, a family’s life is upended by the rapidly declining health of Leslie, a dementia-stricken artist. She’s tended to by both her husband and daughter, but the two caregivers butt heads over Leslie’s best interests. This deeply touching drama was awarded with the Silver Bear Jury Prize at the Berlinale.
description: This Silver Bear winner is uncompromising, charged and claustrophobic, refusing to offer easy answers to existential questions.

imdb.title: Queen at Sea
imdb.plot: As dementia erodes a woman's ability to communicate her inner life, her husband and daughter struggle to act in her best interest, navigating love and the fragile boundaries between care, protection, and autonomy.

films.title: Barbara Forever
intro: Forever is a long time, but thanks to Brydie O’Connor’s confident debut feature the work of queer cinema pioneer Barbara Hammer might enter enternity. Drawing on five decades of radical self-documentation, Barbara Forever traces an artist who transformed her body, relationships and politics into a groundbreaking new language of queer film.
description: Barbara Forever immortalises the work of the pioneering lesbian filmmaker Barbara Hammer, who passed away in 2019. Even more so than this debut by Brydie O’Connor, it was Hammer herself who documented her own life. Over the course of five decades, she made over eighty experimental films with and about herself. A wellspring of ideas, she captured not only her own body and queerness on film, but also her passionate relationships, her thirst for recognition, her cancer diagnosis and the bond she forged with the younger filmmaker Joey Carducci. “It’s more than a life, it’s a history of queer art,” says the ever-energetic Hammer about her own influential career. As well as introducing us to and paying tribute to the woman herself, this inspiring documentary is also a delightful nod to Hammer’s avant-garde aesthetic, which introduced a new queer cinematic language.

imdb.title: Barbara Forever
imdb.plot: An archive-driven exploration of the life, work, and legacy of iconic, pioneering lesbian filmmaker Barbara Hammer.

films.title: Paper Tiger
intro: James Gray returns to a New York crime saga with Paper Tiger. Set in Queens in 1986 and starring a searing Adam Driver and Miles Teller, this tragic thriller follows two brothers whose pursuit of the American Dream draws them into the ruthless world of the Russian mafia. A richly textured family drama about loyalty, toxic ambition and the price of impossible dreams.
description: After venturing into genres including science fiction (Ad Astra) and coming-of-age (Armageddon Time), director James Gray returns to the crime thriller genre that first put him on the map. In the gripping Paper Tiger – partly inspired by his own childhood – he follows two New York brothers in 1986. Ex-cop Gary and engineer Irwin are chasing the American Dream and see their chance to make a fortune, but are swept up in the ruthless world of the Russian mafia, which puts their family ties to the test. With Adam Driver, Miles Teller and Scarlett Johansson in the lead roles, Gray transforms the familiar contours of the mafia film into an intimate portrait of loyalty and shattered dreams. Rich in detail and steeped in the atmosphere of 1980s Queens, Paper Tiger reaffirms Gray’s status as one of America’s great chroniclers of torn families and the illusions that fuel our drive for success.

films.title: Rehearsals for a Revolution
intro: In her compelling directorial feature film debut, actress and filmmaker Pegah Ahangarani intertwines her personal story with over four decades of Iranian history. Through five portraits of family members and mentors, she combines personal archives, family footage and historical material to paint an intimate portrait of a country shaped by repression and a lasting desire for change.
description: How to tell the history of a country when it is inextricably linked to your own family history? In her poignant directorial feature film debut, actress and filmmaker Pegah Ahangarani brings more than forty years of Iranian history to the screen, from the 1979 revolution to the war of 2026. Through five portraits of family members and mentors, she explores various forms of resistance and the people who have shaped her. Using a rich collage of personal archives, family footage, voice recordings, news clips and protest footage, Ahangarani weaves together individual and collective memories. In doing so, she paints a picture of a country marked by political oppression, yet also by an enduring desire for change. Rehearsals for a Revolution is at once a family story, a self-portrait and a chronicle of a country in which generations continue to hope for a revolution that is repeatedly postponed.

In 2026, Willemsfonds, a socio-cultural volunteer organisation, is placing human rights at the heart of its activities. Fundamental rights are under pressure worldwide. Through a film series supported by deMens.nu, Willemsfonds is drawing attention to human rights and their significance in our daily lives. Following the screening on 12 October, Jasmine Malekzadem and Mahdieh Fahimi will discuss the situation in Iran, where various human rights are being violated.

films.title: Siri Hustvedt - Dance Around the Self
intro: Book by book, a detailed and playful portrait is painted of Siri Hustvedt, the celebrated American novelist and essayist. With her deep love of the written word always at its heart, this moving documentary captures both the highs and lows (and the quiet moments of fragile beauty in between) in the life of an author whose body of work continues to expand lavishly.
description: After her portraits of Nan Goldin and Emma Thompson, German filmmaker Sabine Lidl turns her camera on Siri Hustvedt, the celebrated American author of acclaimed novels such as What I Loved (2003) and The Blazing World (2014). Lidl takes us from Hustvedt’s childhood in quiet Minnesota to her arrival in bustling Manhattan, with just one suitcase and five boxes of books. There, she would build a life with the late Paul Auster, as life partners and each other’s most devoted first readers. Hustvedt speaks candidly about the questions, dreams and hunger for more that have continued to shape her writing. “If I could fill my head with the wisdom and art of the ages I would over time augment myself, volume by volume, into the giant I wanted to be,” Hustvedt declared as an aspiring author. Lidl succeeds brilliantly in bringing that literary giant down to human scale in a fitting portrait.

films.title: Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall
intro: For one night, Cameron Winter took over Carnegie Hall. Alone at a Steinway, the Geese frontman and solo artist turned the legendary concert hall into an intimate stage, revealing the full range of a performer who is by turns commanding, vulnerable, strange and unexpectedly funny.
description: On December 11, 2025, Carnegie Hall was packed for a solo concert by Cameron Winter, one of the most elusive voices of his generation. Cameras moved among the audience. Paul Thomas Anderson was there too, in the midst of his Oscar campaign for One Battle After Another. Months later, we get a concert film by two singular voices: Cameron Winter in front of the camera, Paul Thomas Anderson behind it.Over the past two years, Winter has been impossible to ignore. As the frontman of Geese, with Getting Killed one of the most talked-about guitar records of recent years, and as a solo artist with the enigmatic Heavy Metal, he has emerged as a musician who defies every category. The fact that he has earned the admiration of songwriters such as Jeff Tweedy and Nick Cave – who has publicly sung Winter’s praises – perhaps says it all.Few have done what Winter did that night: give a solo concert at Carnegie Hall. Bob Dylan was one of them. Bent over his Steinway, Winter fills the hall with a voice that is almost impossible to capture on record. But just when he reaches the sublime, he seems determined to undercut it himself: with a muttered word, an awkward line, an unexpected turn. His beauty never comes without a wink.Anderson shoots on 16mm and 35mm, with Benny Safdie (The Smashing Machine, FFG2025) behind the camera, and captures that contradiction perfectly. He doesn’t turn Winter into an untouchable rock star, but allows him to be strange, funny and vulnerable. During the breathtaking $0, time seems to stand still for a moment inside Carnegie Hall. In his version of The Rolling Stones, he teases the audience with playful piano noodling. The tension built up throughout Drinking Age is released with his thunderous “From now on this is who I'm gonna be”. And in Love Takes Miles, we hear one of those beautiful, offhand lines Winter is so good at: “Love will make you fit it all in the car.”Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall is a concert film to treasure. Anderson captures the energy of Winter’s songs while bringing his strange, almost cabaret-like presence vividly to the screen. He is virtuosic, awkward and at times deeply moving – often within the same song. The result is a rare document of a once-in-a-lifetime performer.

imdb.title: Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall
imdb.plot: Paul Thomas Anderson captures Brooklyn musician Cameron Winter's minimalist performance in this striking concert film, blending intimate close-ups with sweeping shots of the vast venue, all shot on 16mm and 35mm film.

films.title: Meeuwen sterven in de haven (Seagulls Die in the Harbour)
intro: Regarded as the landmark that launched Flemish arthouse cinema, Meeuwen sterven in de haven follows a drifter haunted by a terrible crime. Wandering through Antwerp’s docks and backstreets, he searches for redemption while crossing paths with unexpected companions. A striking blend of modernism, noir and jazz-infused atmosphere. A film that stands the test of time.
description: From the 1930s onwards, Flanders has had a small but steady film production, mostly comedies. In 1955, Roland Verhavert, (author) Ivo Michiels and Rik Kuypers shot Seagulls Die in the Harbour with private money, a film later regarded as the first Flemish art-house film. In 1956, the film made it into Competition at Cannes. Seagulls Die in the Harbour follows a man (Julien - father of Matthias - Schoenaerts) who, after a terrible crime, wanders the streets and docks of Antwerp. On this journey, hounded by guilt and feverishly searching for redemption, he meets an orphan and two women. Seagulls Die in the Harbour combines the European film modernism of its era with expressionist lighting, finished off with a touch of film noir. Schoenaerts is magnetic as the lost soul in search of something to hold on to. With a soundtrack featuring, among others, Antwerp jazz legend Jack Sels. Ripe for (re)discovery.
The film was restored by CINEMATEK in 2026.

imdb.title: Meeuwen sterven in de haven

films.title: Youri
intro: When journalist Jan Brokken meets flamboyant Soviet pianist Youri Egorov, an interview blossoms into an extraordinary friendship. Joes Brauers and Levan Gelbakhiani shine in Sander Burger’s warm adaptation of In het huis van de dichter, a moving story of two artists, the freedom to forge your own path and the encounters that can change a life forever.
description: Journalist Jan Brokken (Joes Brauers) gets the chance to interview world-famous pianist Youri Egorov (Levan Gelbakhiani). Having fled the Soviet Union, Youri throws himself wholeheartedly into his music and his newly gained freedom in 1980s Amsterdam. Jan is his opposite: thoughtful and reserved, harbouring a writer's dream he doesn't dare pursue. Yet the two recognise something in each other, and their encounter grows into a close friendship. Sander Burger (De veroordeling) adapts Jan Brokken's autobiographical In het huis van de dichter into a warm portrait of two artists at a turning point in their lives. Brauers and Gelbakhiani lend their friendship both lightness and intimacy. Youri is an ode to an encounter that changes the course of two lives, but also to art as a space for freedom — and to the courage it takes to choose that life.

films.title: A Family (Een Familie)
intro: In Een familie (A Family), Mees Peijnenburg explores how a painful divorce affects not only parents but also their children, sixteen-year-old Nina and fourteen-year-old Eli. Told from both siblings’ perspectives, the film reveals their struggle between anger, loyalty and the need to be seen. A nuanced family drama built on intimate moments rather than big emotional gestures.
description: Earlier this year, Mees Peijnenburg left the Berlinale with a special mention from the youth jury in the 14plus category for his film A Family. In it, he shows how a divorce not only tears the parents apart, but also disrupts the lives of their children: sixteen-year-old Nina and her brother Eli, who is two years her junior. The parents believe that their acrimonious divorce is taking place over their children’s heads, but nothing could be further from the truth. The children want to be heard and seen, and are torn between anger and loyalty. Notably, Peijnenburg first tells the story from Nina’s perspective, then from Eli’s. This dual perspective helps to nuance the situation: no one in the family is solely a victim or solely to blame. What makes Een familie so powerful is that Peijnenburg opts not for grand dramatic gestures, but for small moments in which the consequences of a divorce become apparent.

films.title: Jonah Was Here
intro: When grieving neurologist Bob moves into his late son's student room, the fifty-something finds himself living among his son's friends, habits and half-finished life. Nathalie Teirlinck's sophomore feature, with a captivating Koen De Bouw in the lead role, turns a father's unwillingness to let go into an intimate study of loss.
description: ‘You can’t just clear him out,’ Bob shouts as his ex-wife empties out their late son’s student flat. We all grieve and find comfort in different ways. This is also true for the divorced neurologist, who, overcome by grief, immerses himself in his son’s student room and student life. Suddenly, Bob finds himself back amongst the students, getting to know his son’s flatmates and meeting his son’s suspected crush. Seven years after her poetic debut film Le passé devant nous, director and KASK alumna Nathalie Teirlinck returns with a unique, tender grief-themed drama – partly filmed in Ghent – about a man who stubbornly clings to the last remnants of his son. A simple yet clever screenplay penned by Teirlinck herself supports a tormented Koen De Bouw in the lead role. He shines as the confused, yet recognisable and endearing father. Amidst the student rooms and the belongings left behind, Bob learns that grieving, too, is an art in its own right.

films.title: Talk: Editing Rohmer - Mary Stephen
intro: This year, Film Fest Gent welcomes director and editor Mary Stephen as Guest of Honour for the Classics programme, which is dedicated to the French filmmaker Éric Rohmer. Together with Classics curator Patrick Duynslaegher, she dives into the world of Rohmer.
description: Stephen and Rohmer forged a unique collaboration that lasted more than 25 years: from 1981 right up to his final film, Les Amours d’Astrée et de Céladon (2007). She took her first step into Rohmer’s world as an assistant editor to Cécile Decugis on La femme de l’aviateur — she even made a brief cameo appearance in it. That initial experience developed into a regular collaboration: she served as Rohmer’s regular editor on, amongst others, three of the four films in the Contes des quatre saisons cycle (Conte d’automne, Conte d’été and Conte d’hiver).Their bond extended beyond the editing desk. Rohmer composed the music and sound for his films himself, which Stephen in turn performed – a collaboration that was characteristic of their partnership and for which they even coined the pseudonym ‘Sébastien Erms’. Classics curator Patrick Duynslaegher sits down for a conversation with Mary Stephen, who takes us behind the scenes of Rohmer’s film world and introduces us to the small, close-knit team of which she was a part for many years.One of Stephen’s own films, Ombres de soie (1978), will also be screened during the festival, in the presence of the director herself.

What brings them together is their love and admiration for Rohmer’s films. They will delve deeper into the filmmaker’s screenplays and cinematography, whilst also discussing his unique approach to working with his actors. films.title: Sentiments, Signes, Passions: Een expo over Jean-Luc Godard
intro: A mushroom cloud, legends of film history, IS flags, sunsets in Tunis, scenes of flight, execution and war: Jean-Luc Godard’s at once poëtic and political film Le livre d’image (2018) spans more than a century. It questions the production of images, art, religion, representation and law.
description: The filmmaker combined film and contemporary history in five chapters and an epilogue to create an associative collage. The exhibition Sentiments, Signes, Passions is conceived by Fabrice Aragno, filmmaker and longtime collaborator of Godard. It takes up the division of Le livre d’image into chapters, further fragmenting the parts of the work and unfurling them in space. The dynamic projection breaks with the chronological form of a film screening. Across forty screens, the audience can give free rein to associations and pursue their own visual lines of sight.

This internationally acclaimed project offers a rare window into the creative world of Jean-Luc Godard, inviting visitors to step inside the mind of one of cinema’s most influential figures. Deeply respectful of his mentor, Aragno travels the world with each time a different version of the installation. For Film Fest Gent he adds a new component, documenting Godard’s personal workspace: Et la nuit le jour.

films.title: WSA Film Music Days - The Corporatisation of Screen Music: Saving the Human Composer
intro: In times when artificial intelligence can write a full, usable film score in minutes, what does this leave for the composer? Moderator Thomas Mikusz sits down with COOL Music Group CEO Darrell Alexander and composers Simon Franglen, Martin Phipps and Adiescar Chase for a frank conversation about the corporatisation racing through screen music.
description: Discussing similar practices, such as production-music libraries generating trailers and ad scores from a text prompt, the studios quietly weighing cost against craft, and some Hollywood composers even offering a so-called $1 score, the panelists make a case for keeping human composers at the center of the score.

The pattern we're watching evolves gradually: AI-generated or AI-assisted cues normalise first in the lowest-scrutiny work such as documentaries, daytime television, commercials, and branded content. From there, however, it will inevitably move into games, TV series and, eventually, film. At the end of that pipeline, the word “composer” risks narrowing to “prompt engineer,” working a system trained on other composers' output. Currently, AI is trained on existing copyright, and studios and production companies insist that composers must not use AI to maintain a clean chain of title, but this could change.We're already seeing early signs of it. There are music companies out there that don't seem to celebrate the individual human spirit; they seem to treat scores as a corporate commodity rather than an art form. That produces exactly one thing: generic musical slop, and a race to the bottom. We want to build a case for keeping an individual creative and artistic human composer at the centre of the score, made before someone else gets to decide there doesn't need to be one. If you're a young composer: who do you want deciding what your career looks like? You, or an algorithm?

intro: Director Lukas Dhont, composer Valentin Hadjadj and music supervisor Pierre-Marie Dru sit together to talk about their creative collaboration on the soundtrack for Coward. They explore their role within the musical universe of the film and their previous collaborations.
description: Coward, the official opening film of Film Fest Gent 2026, follows young soldiers Pierre, who newly arrives at the front in the First World War, and Francis, who decides to lift the spirits of his comrades by putting together a theatre show. Coward has been selected as the Belgian entry for the Oscar for Best International Feature Film, and was awarded the prize for Best Actor in Cannes.

The movie’s soundtrack is unique in its combination of an original score with historical archival music. The original score, composed by Hadjadj, who previously collaborated with Dhont on Girl and Close, plays an essential role in balancing the film’s brutal setting with its delicate emotional core. The songs performed by the actors were actually written and performed by soldiers in the trenches, and were dug up from the archives, coordinated by Dru. By combining these two elements, the soundtrack captures both the fragile beauty of the men's theatrical revues and the overwhelming dread of trench warfare. Accompanied by a selection of film clips, the trio discusses the working process and creative decisions that form the backbone of this unique soundtrack.

This talk is moderated by Laura Bell and presented in collaboration with the UK & European Guild of Music Supervisors. intro: During the Composer's Talks, we give a composer the time and space to talk in depth about their oeuvre. They discuss the highlights of their career, their sources of inspiration, and the working process behind their renowned body of work. For the first one-on-one conversation, we invite WSA Lifetime Achievement Award recipient Trevor Jones.
description: Born in Cape Town, South Africa, in 1949, Jones developed an interest in film music at the age of five. He attended the South African College of Music at the University of Cape Town, and at the age of seventeen he moved to London to attend the Royal Academy of Music. He later became a British citizen and continued his studies at the University of York and the National Film and Television School, where he would eventually serve as Chair of Music.

Jones became known for his sweeping orchestral scores, always setting the mood from the very first note. With dark fantasy films like Excalibur (1981), his breakthrough score, and The Dark Crystal (1982) and psychological horror films like Angel Heart (1987) he gained international recognition in the 1980s. Later he went on to score classics like Mississippi Burning (1988), The Last of the Mohicans (1992), and Brassed Off (1996), earning him multiple nominations, including three BAFTA nominations and two Golden Globe nominations.

In addition to film scoring, Jones has collaborated widely in the music industry. He worked with David Bowie on the soundtrack for Labyrinth (1986) and has produced or collaborated with artists including U2, Elvis Costello, Sting and Sinéad O’Connor. He has also written music for theatre and concert music, and he has been a regular jury member and guest lecturer at major film and music institutions.

intro: Put on a VR headset and step into the life of a lesbian in Iris Van der Meule’s Lesbian Simulator. Create your own avatar and experience coming out, queer dating, prejudice, discrimination and verbal abuse, but also love, humor, celebration and community. The playful game challenges assumptions and celebrates love in all its forms.

description: Put on a pair of VR goggles and step into the life of a lesbian. That’s what Iris Van der Meule promises with Lesbian Simulator. This VR experience is structured like a game. You create your own lesbian avatar and then navigate through various challenging situations. Experience what it means to come out or to go on a date as a queer person. You’ll also encounter the less pleasant aspects: what prejudice, discrimination or verbal abuse feel like. Lesbian Simulator makes it clear that social acceptance is still far from a given. Fortunately, there’s also plenty of room for love, humour, celebration and the warm embrace of the queer community. With her colourful, playful approach, Iris Van der Meule transforms a serious social issue into an interactive game that doesn’t just let you watch, but lets you experience it for yourself. Lesbian Simulator is an invitation to both examine your own prejudices and celebrate love in all its forms.

intro: Honeyboys is a surreal VR experience exploring delivery culture, online consumption and the gig economy. You follow a naked courier descending deeper into a relentless system with no escape or free will. Inspired by lockdown-era China, it offers a confronting yet fascinating journey, enhanced by Spinvis’s striking soundscape.

Honeyboys is a Virtual Reality installation. Order a ticket for the desired show (35 min.) between 14:00 and 22:00 on one of the festival dates (on 11.10 starting from 17:00). Upon arrival, you will be given a headset. 6 places are available per show.
description: Honeyboys takes you through an unbroken series of scenes centred on the world of delivery services, online consumption and the "gig economy" (no steady job, just piecework). The central figure is a naked delivery boy, descending ever deeper into the underbelly of consumer society. The idea arose when the makers – director Tibor De Jong and animator Doris Konings – heard about a Chinese city whose economy came to a complete standstill during the Covid lockdown, except for delivery drivers and livestreamers. The former delivered the products the latter promoted and sold. And so it went on. Honeyboys confronts you with the underside of the gig economy without offering any solution. As a viewer, you have no free will; instead, you're swept along in the whirlpool, so you feel what it's like to be trapped inside such a system. Confronting? Certainly. But fascinating too, with gorgeous sound design by Spinvis.

intro: During the Nominees Round Table, this year’s World Soundtrack Award nominees sit down together for a conversation about their nominated score.
description: The nominees in the categories of Film Composer of the Year, Television Composer of the Year, Best Original Song, Discovery of the Year, Public Choice, and Game Music discuss what it takes to write scores that stand out in the mass of music written in the past year. For some, it is their very first World Soundtrack Award nomination. For others, it is yet another acknowledgement of their talent.

Moderator Loren Sunderland is the founder of Blank House, a creative brand agency specialising in elevating the careers of the world’s award-winning composers through strategy, storytelling, and visual identity. She is also the founder and editor of The Blank Mag, an online publication redefining composer culture through stories and interviews with music-makers globally.

films.title: Producers Talk: Rebecca O'Brien
intro: Rebecca O’Brien has been working as an independent producer for thirty-five years. Prior to that, she gained experience in the industry in a variety of roles: she was location manager on My Beautiful Laundrette (Stephen Frears, 1985) and production manager on several early Channel 4 films.
description: As a producer, she has worked alongside Ken Loach to build one of the most consistent bodies of work in European cinema: Land and Freedom, The Wind That Shakes the Barley, I, Daniel Blake and The Old Oak. Two of these — The Wind That Shakes the Barley (2006) and I, Daniel Blake (2016) — won the Palme d’Or at Cannes. In an interview, she discusses what it takes to get socially engaged stories made and seen, and why those stories matter in dark times.

The moderator for this talk is Hans Everaert, a Belgian film producer and founder of the production company Menuetto. He produced, amongst others, La Civil ( FFG2021), The Eight Mountains (2022), Girl (FFG2018) and Heysel 85 (2026).

films.title: Director's Talk: El Pampero Cine
sections: Focus on: El Pampero Cine: Infinite Stories
intro: El Pampero Cine has always challenged conventional ideas about how films are made and who gets to make them. In this Director’s Talk, Mariano Llinás and Agustín Mendilaharzu reflect on the collective practices, artistic influences and alternative production models that have shaped their work.
description: What does it mean to make a film without fixed roles, hierarchies or a single author at the helm? Mariano Llinás and Agustín Mendilaharzu discuss El Pampero Cine’s collaborative practice, alternative production models and the question of who actually makes a film. From the collective theatre practice of Piel de Lava to the fantastic literature of Borges, Bioy Casares and Silvina Ocampo, literature, theatre, music and cinema constantly flow into one another. How do these cross-pollinations shape their way of telling stories and thinking about authorship?
This Director's Talk will be held in English.

films.title: Marcel Roos, reizend reporter, explorateur, avonturier, cineast
intro: In the 1950s, the Ghent-based explorer, adventurer and filmmaker Marcel Roos was a household name in Belgium and the Netherlands. He made films about his expeditions in South America and wrote travel reports and books on the subject. Like many of his colleagues, he introduced his own films himself, all over the country, and as an enthusiastic presenter, he sought to engage with the audience. The public devoured these ‘discover the world’ films with great enthusiasm. The genre was particularly popular in Flemish cinemas before the advent of television. To mark the publication of his book De schitterende toekomst van Hemelings en zoon, Erik Martens brings the forgotten filmmaker Marcel Roos back into the spotlight. In his film lecture, he engages in conversation with Roos’s predecessors and successors, and we will watch excerpts from his filmography, digitised and restored by Cinematek.

films.title: WSA Film Music Days - From Policy To Practice: A Discussion With The European Composer & Songwriter Alliance
intro: Cinema and screen music may arise from artistic ambitions, but always take shape within a political framework. In this talk, the European Composer & Songwriter Alliance (ECSA) sheds light on the impact of legislation on composer’s rights, the influence of streaming services, and the persistent inequality within the music industry.
description: Together with Sarah Glennane, ECSA president Helienne Lindvall, composers Luis Ivars and Tina Pepper, and Air-Edel Managing Director Maggie Rodford elaborate on how audiovisual legislation can inadvertently impact the composer’s daily artistic practice. Whether they have the rights to perform their own music, are able to share in the success of their work, or can afford to speak up for themselves. The growing use of artificial intelligence and data driven algorithms undeniably influences the composer’s position as an autonomous artist and the ecosystem as a whole, leading to a decrease of (musical) diversity. As a European non-profit, ECSA continues to raise awareness on these malpractices.

The European Composer & Songwriter Alliance (ECSA), founded in 2007 and based in Brussels, is committed to defending and promoting the rights and interests of music authors on a national, European and international level. They advocate for fair commercial terms and work to strengthen the social and economic development of music creation. With 57 member organisations from 29 European countries and a wide range of stakeholders from various cultural and creative sectors, ECSA represents more than 30,000 composers and songwriters. The organisation is this year’s recipient of the WSA Industry Award.

films.title: Double Bill Céline Sciamma: This is How a Child Becomes a Poet / Tutti Frutti
intro: What happens when a filmmaker picks up her camera without knowing where it will take her? In TUTTI FRUTTI (2026), Céline Sciamma (Petite maman, FFG2022) brings together fragments she has been filming since 2022. She conceived the project as her own ‘secret’: a personal space in which she could explore her struggles with the world and rediscover the pure joy of filmmaking. Unlike her meticulously crafted screenplays, she let the film unfold organically: she followed her curiosity and only discovered, during the editing process, which stories lay hidden within the footage. From this freedom emerges her ‘accidental cinema’, in which birdsong, archive footage, AI and the presence of Adèle Haenel come together in a reflection on solidarity, activism and disappearance. TUTTI FRUTTI is screened alongside This Is How a Child Becomes a Poet (2022), her tender tribute to Patrizia Cavalli.

films.title: Barbara Hammer: A Short Film Retrospective
intro: “Touching another woman’s body changed my life,” said avant-garde pioneer Barbara Hammer (1940–2019). “It had to be shown.” When she came out as a lesbian in the early 1970s, she reinvented herself through the Seventh Art. Hammer broke with the visual language of the seventies, placing lesbian desire and female experience at the centre. Not merely as subject matter, but as form: her films pulse, flicker and breathe, as if they were living bodies themselves.

films.title: De Jeugdalliantie: kijken bij de buren
description: 2:30 pm – Together for Dutch-Language Children's FilmDutch-Flemish panel discussion on the importance of film education

Earlier this year, a group of Dutch filmmakers with a big heart for the youngest audiences founded the Jeugdalliantie (Youth Alliance), a think tank that aims to strengthen the position of Dutch productions for children and young people. These films once had a rock-solid reputation, but maintaining that level has proven difficult. Visibility is declining, international competition is growing, and financing is complex. By creating opportunities to meet, developing solutions and sharing advice (solicited or not), the alliance seeks to push youth productions higher up the agenda. One way to achieve this is through film education. Children and young people deserve to discover film as an art form. The Jeugdalliantie hopes to foster a generation that engages with media consciously and creatively, and that will embrace Dutch children's film even more.
Now, for the first time, the Jeugdalliantie is crossing the border to exchange experiences with its Flemish colleagues. What can they do for one another?
Panellists: Vincent Bal, director; Meikeminne Clinckspoor, director and screenwriter; Tijs van Marle, screenwriter; Iris Verhoeven, director of JEF

films.title: Schermen met Cultuur
description: Prof. Dr. Kris Rutten and doctoral researcher and teaching assistant Amanda Adam from the research group 'Culture & Education' (Faculty of Psychology and Pedagogical Sciences at Ghent University) wrote "Schermen met Cultuur" (Screens with Culture) as an intergenerational dialogue about cultural experience and mediation in the age of screens. Through it, they investigate how culture today is also shared and experienced on and through screens. The book draws from experiences collaborating on cultural initiatives, such as Film Fest Gent's Teacher's Day, and offers inspiration for further engaging with cultural experience in education and beyond.

In connection with the book presentation, they invite diverse cultural players—from curators and audience engagement staff to artists and dramaturgs—to participate in a panel discussion about the broader opportunities, challenges, and future of culture and arts education and mediation in Flanders today.

films.title: 26th WSA Ceremony & Concert
intro: On Saturday 10 October, the 26th WSA Ceremony & Concert, where composers get the spotlight they deserve, takes place at Muziekcentrum De Bijloke. Join us for a night full of awards and live music performed by Brussels Philharmonic, conducted by Dirk Brossé.
description: Icelandic Innovation: Hildur Guðnadóttir as Guest of Honour

To celebrate the art of composing for screen, Film Fest Gent’s screen music prizes are home to an international audience for the 26th year in a row. For this year’s edition, we welcome the visionary composer Hildur Guðnadóttir as Guest of Honour. Through an innovative mix of genres and unique experiments, Guðnadóttir takes screen music outside of its traditional borders. The Icelandic composer has scored various soundtracks for films, television and games including Joker (2019), 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple (2016), TÁR (2022), the HBO series Chernobyl (2019) and the first-person shooter game Battlefield 2042 (2021).Lifetime Achievement Award for Trevor Jones

This year, we honour the legendary composer Trevor Jones with a Lifetime Achievement Award. Throughout his career, the South-African composer has created orchestral, rock and electronic scores for countless films and television projects, including The Last of the Mohicans (1992), Notting Hill (1999) and Mississippi Burning (1988). Besides his collaboration with David Bowie for Labyrinth (1986), Jones has worked with several other renowned artists like Sting and Sinéad O’Connor.Music and awards

In addition to a selection of our guest’s music, which will be performed live by Brussels Philharmonic and conducted by maestro Dirk Brossé, the WSA Concert & Ceremony presents awards in the following categories: Film Composer of the Year, Television Composer of the Year, Best Original Song, Discovery of the Year, Best Original Composition by a Young Composer (powered by Vienna Synchron Stage), Public Choice Award, Game Music Award, and Belgian Film Composer of the Year (powered by Sabam).Tickets for the WSA Ceremony & Concert are included in the WSA Industry Packages.
